points.quote: The workbench is the window manager for the app. It owns the main area (one or more side-by-side views) and the right sidebar. The code is in `packages/frontend/core/src/modules/workbench`.

`Workbench` (`entities/workbench.ts`) holds `views$`, `activeViewIndex$` and `activeView$`. ... Its methods include `open`, `newTab`, `openDoc`, `close`, `moveView` and `resize`. ... `View` (`entities/view.ts`) is one managed window.
It has its own history (`createNavigableHistory`), plus `location$`, `entries$`, `title$` and `icon$`. It also has `push`, `replace`, `go` and query-string helpers

`ViewRoot` creates a private `createMemoryRouter(routes)` for each view. A layout effect calls `viewRouter.navigate(location)` whenever the view's `location$` changes. So the view's own history, not the browser URL, decides which route renders.

A route component declares `<ViewHeader>`, `<ViewBody>` and `<ViewSidebarTab>`. These are the Provider halves of the "islands" in `view-islands.tsx`. They portal their content into the matching Targets.
Exactly one view is active. The active view's URL is treated as the URL of the whole app.
Sidebar tabs go into the view's `sidebarTabs$`. `WorkbenchSidebar` shows only the active view's sidebar, with a switcher when the view has several tabs.

Each view keeps its own history stack. `browser-adapter.ts` binds the active view to the browser router: ... If its state points at a key already in the view's entries, the view calls `history.go(delta)`. That is how browser back/forward moves the view.
